title: ABO Discrepancies: Four Types and the Workup
summary: When the front and back of an ABO type disagree, sort the cause into four types — weak antibodies, weak antigens, sticky proteins or miscellaneous — and work it up step by step, from repeat testing to prewarm and saline replacement.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 40 Hit 14 (discrepancy Groups I–IV and workup) and Trap 6 (clear cold autoantibodies and rouleaux before rare causes). Classification and workup checked against Desai 2023; prewarm technique against Raghuwanshi 2020. The reviewer’s specific examples Wharton’s jelly, acquired B, chimerism and cis-AB are not taught here.

objectives: Recognize an ABO discrepancy and state what to report and transfuse while it is unresolved.
Classify discrepancies into Types I–IV with typical causes.
Order the workup and match rouleaux, cold autoantibodies and weak antibodies to their resolution techniques.

scenes.title: The front and the back disagree
scenes.altText: Forward-typing tubes (patient cells + anti-A, anti-B) are both negative, so the cells look group O. Reverse-typing tubes (patient plasma + A1 cells, B cells) should then both be 4+ — but both are negative. A red “Discrepancy” stamp appears between the two halves.

cues.text: Forward typing: the patient’s red cells don’t react with anti-A or anti-B. The cells look like group O.
A group O person should have anti-A and anti-B in their plasma. But the reverse typing shows no reaction with A1 or B cells.
Front and back disagree. That is an ABO discrepancy, and you can’t report a blood group until it’s solved.

scenes.title: Normal: forward and reverse must agree
scenes.altText: A matched group A result: forward anti-A 4+, anti-B 0; reverse A1 cells 0, B cells 4+. A green check links the two halves. Then a rule card: when they don’t agree, record every result, delay the final interpretation, and if the patient needs blood now, give group O red cells until it is resolved.

cues.text: Here is a normal group A. Forward: the cells react with anti-A, not anti-B.
Reverse: the plasma contains anti-B, so it agglutinates B cells but not A1 cells. The two halves agree.
When they don’t agree, record every result and hold the final interpretation until the discrepancy is resolved.
If the patient needs red cells before then, give group O red cells. For a donor, the unit is quarantined.

props.title: If they disagree
lines: Record all results · hold the interpretation
Patient needs blood now → group O red cells

scenes.title: What changes: four kinds of discrepancy
scenes.altText: Four cards appear in turn. Type I — weak or missing antibodies (reverse side): infants, the elderly, hypogammaglobulinemia, recent marrow transplant. Type II — weak or missing antigens (forward side): ABO subgroups, leukemia. Type III — plasma-protein problems causing rouleaux or pseudoagglutination, e.g. myeloma; a stack of red cells like coins illustrates rouleaux. Type IV — miscellaneous: cold autoantibodies, unexpected alloantibodies, Bombay phenotype.

cues.text: Type one: the antibodies are weak or missing, so the reverse type is too weak. Think of newborns — anti-A and anti-B develop after about 4 to 6 months — and the elderly, people with low immunoglobulins, or a recent marrow transplant.
Type two: the antigens are weak or missing, so the forward type is too weak. Think ABO subgroups, and leukemia, which can weaken A and B antigens.
Type three: abnormal plasma proteins, as in myeloma, make red cells stack like coins. These rouleaux look like agglutination, giving false-positive reactions.
Type four is everything else: cold autoantibodies, unexpected alloantibodies, and rare phenotypes such as Bombay.

props.title: I · weak/missing antibodies
lines: Infants · elderly · low IgG · marrow transplant

scenes.title: In the lab: working it up
scenes.altText: A numbered workup path lights up: 1 repeat the test on the same sample; 2 check reagents and equipment; 3 get a fresh sample and retest; 4 review previous blood-group records; 5 review the patient’s history (age, diagnosis, transplant, medications); 6 add special serology (adsorption–elution, saliva studies). Side tools: rouleaux → saline replacement; cold antibodies → prewarm and test at 37 °C; weak antibodies → enhance the reverse type (more plasma, longer incubation, colder temperature). A tube of rouleaux clears to 0 after saline replacement.

cues.text: Start simple. Repeat the test on the same sample, then check the reagents and the equipment. Many discrepancies are technical.
Still there? Get a fresh sample and retest — a wrong-blood-in-tube can look like a discrepancy. Check previous records.
Then read the history: age, diagnosis, transplant, medications. Special tests like adsorption–elution or saliva studies come last.
Specific fixes: rouleaux disperse with saline replacement — the plasma is replaced with saline, and false clumps fall apart.
Cold autoantibodies are handled by prewarming and testing at 37 degrees. Weak antibodies can be boosted with more plasma, longer incubation, or a colder temperature.

props.label: Wrong blood in tube can mimic a discrepancy
Weak antibody → more plasma, longer, colder

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Unexpected reverse-type agglutination = rare subgroup” is crossed out → “Rule out the common causes first: cold autoantibodies (prewarm) and rouleaux (saline replacement).” Trap card: “Missing reverse reactions in a 2-month-old = discrepancy to work up” is crossed out → “Expected: anti-A and anti-B develop after about 4–6 months; reverse typing is usually not done on newborns.”

cues.text: Trap one: the reverse type shows extra agglutination, and you jump to a rare subgroup. Clear the common causes first: cold autoantibodies and rouleaux. Prewarm, and try saline replacement.
Trap two: a two-month-old has no reverse reactions. That is expected. Anti-A and anti-B develop after about 4 to 6 months, so reverse typing is usually not done on newborns.
And never report a blood group while a discrepancy is unresolved. Group O red cells bridge the gap.

props.title: ✗ “No reverse reactions at 2 months = work it up.”

props.label: Unresolved → don’t report · give group O red cells

scenes.title: Back weak, front weak, sticky, strange
scenes.altText: Memory aid: four doors. I “Back weak” (antibodies), II “Front weak” (antigens), III “Sticky” (proteins → rouleaux), IV “Strange” (cold autoantibodies, alloantibodies, Bombay). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: back weak, front weak, sticky, strange. One: the back — antibodies — is weak. Two: the front — antigens — is weak. Three: sticky proteins. Four: strange extras.
Where it breaks: textbooks number and name these groups differently, one patient can have more than one cause, and the categories describe the pattern — they don’t replace the stepwise workup.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “Forward ≠ reverse → don’t report; give group O red cells”, “I antibodies · II antigens · III proteins · IV miscellaneous”, “Repeat → fresh sample → history; prewarm, saline replacement”.

cues.text: When forward and reverse typing disagree, hold the result and give group O red cells, sort the cause into weak antibodies, weak antigens, protein problems or miscellaneous, and work it up from repeat testing to special serology.

props.label: Forward ≠ reverse → don’t report · give group O red cells
I antibodies · II antigens · III proteins · IV miscellaneous
Repeat → fresh sample → history · prewarm · saline replacement

explanation.what: Plain language: the blood group is tested two ways — the cells and the plasma — and both must point to the same group. Scientific terms: an ABO discrepancy is disagreement between cell (forward) and serum/plasma (reverse) grouping; it is classified as Type I (weak or missing antibodies), Type II (weak or missing antigens), Type III (protein or plasma abnormalities causing rouleaux or pseudoagglutination) or Type IV (miscellaneous, e.g. cold or unexpected antibodies, Bombay).
explanation.why: Anti-A and anti-B develop after about 4–6 months of age and can fall with ageing, hypogammaglobulinemia or after marrow transplant; leukemia can weaken A and B antigens through reduced glycosyltransferase activity; paraproteins cause rouleaux; cold autoantibodies agglutinate at room temperature.
explanation.measure: Workup: repeat on the same sample, check reagents and equipment, test a fresh sample, review previous records and the medical history, then special serology (adsorption–elution, saliva studies). Rouleaux: saline replacement. Cold antibodies: prewarm and test at 37 °C. Weak antibodies: increase the serum-to-cell ratio and extend incubation, including at 4 °C.
explanation.differs: True agglutination vs rouleaux (disperses with saline replacement); expected absent reverse reactions in newborns vs a true discrepancy; reporting a group vs holding the result and giving group O red cells.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: assign a pattern to Types I–IV, the infant reverse-typing exception, rouleaux in myeloma resolved by saline replacement, cold autoantibodies resolved by prewarming, and what to transfuse while unresolved.

comparisons.title: Type I vs Type II
comparisons.distinguisher: Which half of the type is weaker than expected.

comparisons.title: Rouleaux vs agglutination
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether the clumps fall apart when plasma is replaced with saline.

mnemonic.text: Back weak, front weak, sticky, strange.
mnemonic.explanation: Type I: the back (reverse, antibodies) is weak; Type II: the front (forward, antigens) is weak; Type III: sticky proteins (rouleaux); Type IV: strange extras (cold autoantibodies, alloantibodies, Bombay).
mnemonic.limitation: Textbooks number and name the groups differently, one patient can have several causes, and the categories never replace the stepwise workup.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old with multiple myeloma types as forward group A, but the plasma agglutinates both A1 and B cells (2+). The cells look like stacks of coins under the microscope. What is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat the reverse type using saline replacement
options.rationale: Correct. Paraproteins cause rouleaux (a Type III discrepancy); saline replacement disperses rouleaux but not true agglutination.
Incorrect. The forward type is A; the reverse reactions are likely false positives from rouleaux.

options.text: Perform subgroup studies with anti-A1 lectin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Subgroups are a forward-side (Type II) problem; clear the common protein cause first.
Incorrect. The cells react with anti-A; nothing supports group O.

questions.stem: A patient’s forward type shows weak reactions with anti-A, while the reverse type shows anti-B only. The patient has acute leukemia. Which discrepancy type is this?

options.text: Type II — weak or missing antigens
options.rationale: Correct. Leukemia can weaken A and B antigens, making the forward type too weak.

options.text: Type I — weak or missing antibodies
options.rationale: Incorrect. The reverse type (antibodies) is as expected; the forward side is weak.
Incorrect. Type III gives extra reactions (rouleaux), not weak antigen reactions.
Incorrect. Unexpectedly weak reactions are a discrepancy and must be resolved before reporting.

questions.stem: A patient with an unresolved ABO discrepancy needs red cells urgently. What should be issued?

options.rationale: Correct. Group O red cells lack A and B antigens, so they are safe while the discrepancy is resolved.

options.text: Red cells matching the forward type
options.rationale: Incorrect. The forward type may be wrong; that is why there is a discrepancy.
Incorrect. AB red cells carry A and B antigens and are compatible only with AB recipients.

options.text: Nothing until the discrepancy is resolved
options.rationale: Incorrect. Urgent transfusion should not wait; group O red cells bridge the gap.

claims.text: Type I weak/missing antibodies; Type II weak/missing antigens; Type III protein abnormalities (rouleaux); Type IV miscellaneous (cold or unexpected antibodies, Bombay).
Record all results, postpone interpretation, quarantine donor units, give group O red cells to recipients until resolved.
Workup: repeat → reagents/equipment → fresh sample → records → history → adsorption–elution/saliva.

Type I in infants (antibodies after 4–6 months), elderly, hypogammaglobulinemia, marrow transplant; Type II in leukemia; rouleaux resolved by saline replacement; weak antibodies enhanced by more serum, longer incubation, 4 °C.
Cold autoantibodies are resolved by prewarming and testing at 37 °C.
ABO subgroups cause Type II discrepancies; myeloma paraproteins cause rouleaux.
claims.note: Desai reports weak ABO variants in donors and rouleaux cases, but does not name subgroups as Type II or myeloma as the protein source.

claims.text: Cold autoantibodies and rouleaux are more common causes than cis-AB, chimerism or acquired B.
claims.note: Plausible from Desai’s case mix (rouleaux 28/96, cold 9/96) but no source compared these with cis-AB or acquired B.

claims.text: Doors, stacked-coin rouleaux and tube reactions.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer’s workup order (ID recheck → prewarm → saline replacement → lectins → subgroup studies) differs from Desai 2023 (repeat → reagents → fresh sample → records → history → special serology); the lesson teaches Desai’s general order and the technique-to-cause matches.

morphology.note: Tubes and the rouleaux stack are schematic; review real images of rouleaux vs agglutination.
